en: The *Vīrūpākṣapañcāśikā*,
together with the commentary composed by Vidyācakravartin.
Homage to the one whose body is the universe, who manifests as the singular identity of all.
To Śambhu, for the sake of constant self-reflection and for the accomplishment of the universe.
We shall provide an exposition of the *Pañcāśikā* spoken by Virūpākṣa, which consists of a compendium of the essential meanings established in the doctrine of consciousness (*saṃvitsiddhānta*).

In this world, the illustrious Lord Paramaśiva Bhaṭṭāraka, whose sole delight is in bestowing grace upon the universe, having assumed a form for sport and wandering under the name of the venerable Śrī Virūpākṣanātha, once—
Having approached the Lord of the gods— who considers himself the possessor of supreme sovereignty and whose battle-elephant is Gandhasindhura—
he [acted] by mere will before him.

When the battle between the two great mountains had been manifested, and [the assembly] there was endowed with a state of total being— its pride in sovereignty having been pacified by the extraordinary curiosity to behold that [battle]—
[he appeared] for the sake of awakening them to it.

He brought forth this *Pañcāśikā* treatise, which constitutes the ultimate quintessence of the entire established doctrine of consciousness (*saṃvit-siddhānta*). Therein, in the first and last [verses]...
Because the two verses constitute the introduction and conclusion,
and because the passage concerning Śuka and Vāmadeva (verse 50) is merely incidental, they do not constitute formal instruction. The remaining [verses]...
The fifty verses constitute its form; thus, this treatise is called the *Pañcāśikā*.
Therein, by means of the first chapter consisting of seven verses beginning with "the point of disagreement," [it treats] that which is perceived as being external to the body.
The fact that the universe constitutes the body [of the Lord] has been established through reasoned arguments. Now,
in order to dispel the delusion regarding the distinction characterized by the relationship between the body and the embodied,
[the author proceeds] with the thirteen verses beginning with "pratyavamarśātmā."

In the second book, the identity of the universe with the Light has been explained at length and analyzed. Now, [the obstacles] such as the impossibility and contrary notions regarding this identity of the universe with the Light, which has been recognized, [are addressed].
The modes of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), intended so that there may be no contact with [the limitations of] objects (*oṣaiḥ saṃsparśo mā bhūt*),
have been demonstrated in detail through the nineteen verses beginning with "I am the one whose light never sets" (*ahameko'nastamitaprakāśa*).
Not by the third chapter; rather, by the fourth chapter,
consisting of eleven verses beginning with "Even that which resides in me," etc., [the author] proceeds by setting forth the modes of cognition for those who are unawakened, awakened, and so forth.

This treatise consists of four sections (*catuḥskandhaka*), as it teaches the path for the manifestation of both higher and lower accomplishments (*siddhi*) and, ultimately, the Great Accomplishment (*mahāsiddhi*).
Specific details regarding these are described here and there throughout the work.
Now we shall explain the text. Therein, in order to introduce the treatise, he composes this introductory framework (*pīṭhikābandha*):
"To Indra, who delights in the battle with the scent-elephant (*gandhagaja*), [the author] has manifested a battle with the pair of mountains."
Being questioned, Virūpākṣa tells him the seed-syllable of his own spiritual attainment. || 1 ||

By the word "asked," it is indicated that Indra possesses the qualification for the instruction on reality (tattva) due to the descent of power (śaktipāta), which is to be inferred from the signs of his inquiry; thus, [the author] speaks and begins to set forth the initiation consisting of verbal instruction (śābdī dīkṣā). || 1 ||

Therein, first, he sets forth a five-membered syllogism to establish that the universe, which is perceived as existing outside the body, is in fact the body itself: 1. [The proposition: The universe is the body. 2. [The reason: Because it is perceived as being within the range of the senses. 3. [The example: Whatever is perceived as being within the range of the senses is the body, as is the case with one's own body. 4. [The application: And this universe is perceived as being within the range of the senses. 5. [The conclusion: Therefore, the universe is the body.
O limb of doubt, this body of mine, which is consciousness itself,
is established as being like a physical lump because it is an object of perception, from the state of emptiness up to the state of *īlā*. (2)
The word "Aṅga" (Friend/Listen) is used to address and draw the disciple's attention.

This entire range of objects of dispute, from the term "void" (*śūnya*) onwards, is [perceived] by you, who identify with the subject (*grāhaka*), as being external to the body; whereas by me, who am of the nature of consciousness, it is perceived as being within the body.

Because it is being perceived, this entire universe—from the state of being without support down to the earth—is the subject of dispute as my body. The reason for this is: "because it is visible. Just as, for you, the physical aggregate is the body because it is visible and delimited by its status as a perceiver, so too [is the universe].

And for me, whose nature is consciousness and who am unlimited, the entire universe is the body because it is an object of perception. Intending to establish the conclusion through the meaning of the application (*upanaya*), he concludes with "it is established" (*siddham*). For this [body] belongs to everyone...

This is an object established by one's own experience: when [the consciousness] becomes oriented toward a specific object of perception, such as a particular form like blue or yellow, then this subject itself also becomes a limited manifestation. And that—
The limitation of manifestation is indeed conditioned solely by the limitation of the object of apprehension. However,
when one synthesizes every single reality in its generality,
then this manifestation, which is of the nature of consciousness, is unlimited.
Because it is impossible for that which illuminates space, time, and so forth to be delimited by space, time, and so forth,
the entire universe is therefore the body, since it is visible at that [time]. If it were not so,
then even the physical aggregate (piṇḍa) would not be a body in the state of the subject (grāhaka).

Because there is no difference in their being objects of perception (*dṛśyatva*). Therefore, when the specific characteristic of being a subject (*grāhakatva*) has dissolved, it is taught that even for you, whose nature is consciousness (*caitanya*), the entire universe is indeed the body.
Now, is it not the case that mere objectivity (*dṛśyatvamātra*) is not the cause for being a body, but rather [the sense of] "I-ness" (*ahantā*)?
[The nature of] being perceived: the physical body is perceived as "I," whereas the universe is perceived as "this. Therefore, how is the stated conclusion established? To this he says:
"I am prosperous, I am emaciated, I have affectionate senses, I am rejoicing."
"I breathe" and "I am empty"—thus is the view of "I-am-ness" (asmitā) observed within these six states. || 3 ||

The property of objects such as houses and fields is *sampad* (prosperity); that of the body is *kārśya* (emaciation); that of the senses such as the eyes is *sneha* (moisture); that of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is *moda* (joy);
that of the vital air (*vāyu*) is *prāṇana* (animation); and that of the state of deep sleep, which is a synonym for *māyā*, is *śūnyatā* (emptiness).
Among these six categories, beginning with objects, the sense of "I-ness" (*asmitā*)— the conceit of "I"— is observed in you as well, established by your own experience. This being the case,
when the conceit of "I" arises toward an object conceived as external to the body, then...

Because it is an object of perception, the body is also an "object" (viṣaya). However, when there is no identification with the "I" (ahaṃkāra), then even the body, senses, and so forth, are not the "body. Therefore, the discrepancy that was suspected—namely, that there is "I-ness" (asmitā) toward the physical aggregate while there is "this-ness" (idantā) toward objects external to it—is [resolved].
The sense is that this is merely a deception caused by a lack of critical inquiry. || 3 ||
Now, even so, it may be objected that egoism (asmitā) is observed only with respect to six specific objects and things, such as the sense-objects, and not everywhere; therefore, he says:
"Egoism is established through the cessation of sense-objects, body, senses, intellect, and vital breath."
Thus, for one who maintains this consciousness throughout the entire path, there is the state of having the universe as one's body.
This "I-ness" (asmitā) which is established in relation to the six [objects], beginning with the sense-objects, belongs only to consciousness (citi),
and not to the grasper, because the latter is submerged in the state of emptiness. Thus, this "I-ness" is established within the six states.

If you maintain your consciousness throughout the entire path, as if it were the sixfold self, and if you firmly cultivate the recognition that all things— from Śiva down to the earth— are eternally pure, then for you too—

The remainder [of the sentence] is that the state of having a universal body will become the object of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). According to the stated method, within the six stages (*pada*), the sense of "I-ness" (*asmitā*) belongs to consciousness (*cit*) alone, and not to the subject (*grāhaka*). Furthermore, since consciousness is of the nature of uninterrupted luminosity, its "I-ness" is restricted to specific [objects].

It is not possible [that it should not occur], yet it occurs everywhere. If you perceive this "I-am-ness" (asmitā) of consciousness— which is eternally established everywhere— with firm realization, then your state of being the body of the universe, which is likewise eternally established, will be realized.
The intended meaning is that there would be recognition (pratyabhijñā). || 4 ||

But surely, according to the principle already stated, it follows that the entire world is the body of the universe; yet this is not seen to be so, because the sense of "I-ness" (ahantā) is firmly established only in the physical body. Therefore, this is established by direct perception.
To the question, "How can the sense of 'I-ness' (abhimantṛtva) regarding the body be otherwise [transformed]? he says:
"Having transcended the entire limb [of the body], one whose sense of 'I' (ahantā) is established in a single part of that [body]."
The world is clearly like one whose life-breath is choking in the throat, as if dead while still living. || 5 ||
Having transcended from everything— the universe consisting of limbs, that is, the body, as well as from all entities such as Śiva and the rest— even while not having actually transcended,
one becomes as if transcended through a lack of self-reflection (*svāvimarśa*).

With the sense of "I" firmly rooted in a particular body— whether divine, human, or animal— which is one specific portion of that [universal] body, he is like one whose life-breath is gasping in his throat.

The world—this multitude of living beings—is clearly dead while yet alive; it truly exists as if it were a living corpse. There is no denial of this fact whatsoever. When the cause for this is investigated, it is none other than *māyā*, characterized by a lack of self-reflection (*svāvimarśa*). However, once such reflection is attained, everything [is transformed].
Śiva alone is the body of the universe. || 5 ||
Therefore, for this reason: just as there is a mutual clashing of two inert arms in the body due to the sense of "I-ness" (asmitā),
so too, by the mere power of will, such a thing occurs even between two mountains in this world.

Just as those who possess the conceit of being perceivers strike their palms against each other within the body by mere will through the sense of "I-ness" (asmitā), so too, for me— the conscious Self—
there is the striking of two mountains in this world by mere force of will through the sense of "I-ness."

It proceeds as follows: the firm conviction "I am" regarding the body and desire—these alone are the cause for clapping one's hands, and not any other cause whatsoever. Likewise, for me too, the firm conviction "I am" regarding the world and desire are the cause for striking the mountain.

Therefore, this lack of sovereignty of yours arises solely from the laxity of your attachment to the world; however, through its firmness, the sovereignty that is eternally established will manifest even for you—this is the intended meaning. || 6 ||
Now, if this is merely a matter of desire, we do not see the accomplishment of the "slapping of the hands" by that alone; rather,
it occurs only when the causal complex characterized by the movements of the *bindu*, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth is present.
Therefore, how is the validity of the stated meaning established? To this he says:

"Entering the drop (bindu), the vital breath (prāṇa), power (śakti), the mind (manas), the circle of the senses, and the body, sustain [them] as they move, and maintain the sense of 'I' everywhere. (7)
The *bindu* is the subtle, general sense of "I" (*ahaṃpratīti*) that flows spontaneously prior to the emergence of specific cognitions such as the subject and the act of grasping;
the *prāṇa* is the vital breath (*asu*) which is the cause of agitation in the internal organs, such as self-conceit (*abhimāna*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*).

By the term "power" (*śakti*), the intellect (*buddhi*) and the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) are included, because they exist as the power-forms of the self through their respective functions of determination (*adhyavasāya*) and self-identification (*abhimāna*). [The Goddess] enters these six objects, beginning with the *bindu*, and causes them to act.
By the power of even a tiny fraction of your own touch, maintain the vibration of the sense of "I" everywhere;
for if you maintain it everywhere by that very same method through which you maintain it with firm conviction in the body, then such perfections as these will be yours.
The meaning is that they remain as eternally established. || 7 ||

Now, is it not the case that this "I-ness" (ahantā) is merely an expansion perfected through mental cultivation, and is not experienced as possessing an excellence of attributes such as lordship (īśvaratva) and agency (kartṛtva)?
Therefore, in order to dispel the doubt as to how such a perfection can possibly occur, he says:
"Sovereignty, agency, independence, and the nature of consciousness."
These, indeed, are said by the wise to be synonyms for egoism (ahaṃtā). || 8 ||
This very "I-ness" (ahantā) which has been recognized by you is itself lordship (īśvaratā),

and it is itself agency (kartṛtva), autonomy (svātantrya), and the nature of consciousness (cinmayatva). Whatever excellence of lordship and so forth is established in the scriptures, all of that consists of this "I-ness."
Thus, terms such as "Lordship" (īśvaratva) and so forth are synonyms and designations.
By this, the lack of conviction regarding the "I-sense" (ahantā)— which is caused by the non-experience of Lordship and the rest— is refuted, in whatever manner [it may have arisen].

It has also been indicated that as the firmness of recognition increases, there is the manifestation of the powers of those who are eternally established, such as their lordship, agency, and so forth; may all be auspicious. 8.
[Thus ends the first chapter, the Investigation into the Universal Body, in the *Vīrūpākṣapañcāśikā* together with its commentary.]
[Now the second chapter:

Having thus established the state of being the body of the universe through the first chapter, [the author now proceeds] to sublate the delusion of distinctions such as the relationship between the body and the embodied self.

The universal nature of Light is commenced in the second chapter. Therein, this consciousness—which flows by its own inherent force and consists of a general form through the dissolution of specific attributes such as subjectivity—is not perceived as "I"; therefore—
Anticipating the question, "How is this 'I-ness' (ahaṃtā)? he says:

"This supreme Speech, which is consciousness whose nature is reflective awareness and which flows by its own inherent force—that is the true I-ness, in which the entire collection of phonemes has been withdrawn from beginning to end. (9)

It has the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), whose essence is the act of retrospection (*pratyavamarśa*). Because it is established through one's own direct experience by everyone, it is appropriately indicated as "this" (*asau*) by way of immediate perception. Consciousness (*citi*) is the abiding of the cognizer in its own essential form, free from the coloring of any object of cognition (*cetya*).
Flowing by its own inherent force (*svarasavāhinī*), constantly vibrating in form due to the absence of any obstruction,
that Speech (*vāk*) consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Even there, because it manifests solely as the light of its own essential nature (*svarūpajyotiṣ*),
this [Speech] is not of the nature of *paśyantī* and so forth— which are distinct from its own essence— but rather [is that very essence itself].

"Since the scripture is indeed the Supreme [Speech], it is the light of its own nature within, the subtle Speech that never departs" (Vākyapadīya Sva-bhāva-kāṇḍa 1.142). Because this [Speech] consists of the nature of pure Speech, it is composed of phonemes through the method of *pratyāhāra* (comprehensive inclusion).
By means of the letters *a* and *ha* taken together, the term *ahantā* is etymologically explained; however, this "I-ness" (*ahantā*) does not exist merely by virtue of being perceived as "I."

Surely, the so-called "I-ness" (ahantā) is the property of the "I" (aham). What other [entity] is perceived that, being distinct from consciousness whose nature is reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa), deserves to be designated as "I"? Therefore—
He said:
That light which is the self capable of illuminating both itself and others, that is called the one "I"; such is its state as "I-ness" (ahantā). (10)

He is that which exists as the very self of the universe— consisting of both the sentient and the insentient— and is capable of manifesting his own nature, which consists of an extracted light, as well as the supreme reality and everything down to the blue object through reflective awareness and so forth.

Light (prakāśa), being one and non-dual because distinctions such as space and time cannot exist within its own nature, is traditionally taught in the scriptures as "I" (aham). Its very state is "I-ness" (ahantā),
which consists of the reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) that was just described.

The intention here is as follows: this light (*prakāśa*), which is of the sole nature of cognition, which illumines everything from the subsequent reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) up to the object "blue" that is to be known, and which partakes in all acts of measurement (*pramiti*), cannot be designated as either "self" or "other."

Because those two are objects of cognition; therefore, it is one alone, since there is no possible means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to differentiate it. In the scriptures, its expression as "I" (*aham*) occurs through the withdrawal of the letters *a* and *ha*.

In that regard, although the term *ahaṃ* (I) consists merely of the verbal root and is meaningful in itself, nevertheless, because the verbal root alone is unfit for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), it is employed in conjunction with the cognition (*pratyaya*) "I. Regarding its status as the cause [of that cognition]:
That which is this state of arisen reflective awareness is "I-ness" (ahantā). || 10 ||

Indeed, we perceive a triad: that which is to be known as "this," the grasper consisting of the notion of "I" (the *ahaṃpratyaya*), and the manifestation (*prakāśa*) just described. To the question, "How is the stated point established? he says:
In him, both the manifestions of "this" and "I"— the interrupted and the uninterrupted—
clearly reveal the states of being the manifested object and the manifesting subject, respectively, in the domains of the cognized and consciousness.
Of that manifested light which has been thus described, there are two properties (*dharma*):
one is discrete, consisting of mutual exclusion, and having the nature of "this"; the other, however, is non-discrete.

This [consciousness] follows from the perspective of "this-first" (idam-prathā). Therein, it clarifies that "this-first" pertains to the state of being manifested (*ābhāsyatā*) in the category of "this" (*cit-pada*), whereas "I-first" (*ahaṃ-prathā*) pertains to the state of manifesting (*ābhāsakatā*) in the category of "consciousness" (*cit-pada*). For "this-first" is expressed as "this is blue," "this is yellow," and so forth.

It consists of mutual exclusion; for as long as that [exclusion] has not extended itself, the manifestability of blue and so forth does not appear. The manifestation of "I," however, is of the nature of persistence, as in the thought, "I know both blue and yellow."
The capacity to manifest [objects] in the state of consciousness (citpada) is based solely on its expansion (tatprathana).
This being the case:
that one [Self] is not [identical] with itself, for here there is no sequence by way of space or time.
In the case of a cognizable object that is mutually differentiated, it is indeed dependent on difference that it is said to be "liberated. (12)

That light is one and indeed non-dual in its very nature as the Self; it is not, however, of a dual form consisting of both the light and the grasper. Now, one might object: "But here and now, there is a sequence in terms of space and time, such that [one thinks], 'I am the grasper. How, then, can there be unity? Anticipating this doubt, he says:

Indeed, there is no sequence here by way of space or time. In this light, there is no sequence or differentiation based on space and time. The reason for this is: that [sequence] is appropriate when objects of cognition are mutually distinct, as in "this is blue" and "this is yellow."

In the object of consciousness (*cetya*) which possesses differentiation, the continuous [awareness] "I know blue and yellow" is appropriate; this very point he makes clear: "For it is indeed based on differentiation. For this [awareness] is precisely the locus of differentiation, which is a property of the object of consciousness. Indeed, what is called "differentiation" is...

The nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛttarūpatā*) is the nature of differentiation, while non-difference (*abhedah*) is the nature of persistence (*anuvṛttarūpatā*). Any distinction created by space and time exists only within the object of cognition; the delusion of difference regarding the state of consciousness (*citpada*), which is the substratum of those distinctions, is based solely upon its limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). || 12 ||

According to the method already stated, there is no difference whatsoever between the light [of consciousness] and the grasper when their essential nature is examined. Now, with the intention that even the object of cognition, when examined, cannot be established as distinct from the light, he says: (Note: The text provided ends with "(-)", indicating a break or the start of a verse. The following is the translation of the preceding prose.)

Within his own limb, which is the self of the sky of consciousness, he creates and destroys the universe through the merging and separation of the waves of his own powers, appearing like milk and rice.
This very Light, within its own limb— its own essential nature which serves as the foundational wall,
consisting of the unconditioned space of consciousness (*cidgagana*)— manifests through the union and differentiation of its own powers in the forms of Khecarī and the rest.
Through the convergence of its rays, by being oriented toward the apprehension of a single object,

it emits and illuminates the world as Śiva and so forth; through their differentiation, by turning away from the apprehended object, it destroys and withdraws it— just as the ocean does through the convergence of its waves.
She creates waves, bubbles, and so forth, and withdraws them through differentiation.
Indeed, prior to the apprehension of objective entities such as Śiva and the rest, there exists only consciousness, which is like the sky;
yet, when there is the desire to manifest [objects], it proceeds through the sequence of the *khecarī*, *gocarī*, and other [powers].

He creates by means of the union of the powers (*śakti*), characterized by their outward orientation through their dedication to a single effect; and when the object has been fully contemplated, he [withdraws it] back into the form of the inner self (*pratyagbhāva*) by means of those same powers, through the sequence of dissolution into the cause.

He withdraws those powers that have attained a state of differentiation within consciousness; for the sake of strengthening the realization that both those powers and that universe do not exist as external to the Light,
he [describes] the powers as being like the waves of the ocean of the Light.

And by the power of the sense, through the state of being waves, the world is metaphorically described as consisting of waves and so forth. Consequently, it is established that when the world, its distinctions, and the powers that constitute its cause are investigated, they are nothing but Light (prakāśa) itself. || 13 ||
Since no entity such as the grasped object and so forth exists separately, and only luminosity exists as the nature of all things,
[this is taught] for the purpose of uprooting the latent impressions of the delusion regarding the distinctions of the grasped object and so forth.
He says that consciousness itself, once recognized through the aforementioned reasoning, should be cultivated for the sake of attaining firm realization:
"In this [world], which consists of the five objects such as form, and which takes the nature of the objects of enjoyment, the senses, and the enjoyer..."
Consciousness, whose infinite wheel of its own powers spreads throughout the world, is to be contemplated.

This entire universe, consisting of the objects of enjoyment, the means of enjoyment, and the enjoyer, when investigated, is found to consist solely of the fivefold objects beginning with form (*rūpa*).
For instance, when form becomes an object as an object of enjoyment, then...

The eye, which effects the apprehension of that [object], as well as the apprehender who consists of that [eye], attains a state of identity with it; and so it is likewise with taste and the other objects. Thus, this world consists of the forms of the objects of enjoyment, the senses, and the enjoyer.
Consciousness (cit) is to be meditated upon as having an infinite wheel of its own powers radiating forth and as an array of various rays of light being set in motion.
By this [it is shown that] objects are infinite; and because they are infinite, meditation upon them is difficult to accomplish.
And thus, those delusions which hold that these [objects] are distinct from consciousness (cid) have been refuted. || 14 ||

Having thus condensed the universe into fivefold and established its nature as consisting of consciousness, he teaches again by condensing it into threefold for the sake of ease in meditation, [affirming] its nature as consisting of consciousness.

The Bindu, characterized by reflection (vimarśa), consists of the moon, sun, fire, the objects of experience, the senses, the enjoyer, and the individual body; it is the one vital breath of the six paths.

The object of enjoyment is characterized by the moon, because it is of the nature of the external (parāc); the senses are characterized by the sun, because they consist of both the external and the internal (pratyag-ātman); the enjoyer is characterized by fire, because its essential nature is solely the internal (pratyag-eka-svabhāva). This [reality] consists precisely of these three.

The universe is nothing other than this. That mass of manifestation (*bhāna-piṇḍa*) belonging to these objects of enjoyment and so forth—which, through the dissolution of specific qualities such as "being an object of enjoyment," consists of a manifestation that is universal in nature and composed of self-reflexive awareness (*vimarśa*)—is called the *bindu*. That *bindu* is one.
Thus, Prāṇa is the self of the six paths, because it is the cause of their arising and resting;
[it is also the self] of the three deities who preside over Soma and the others.
When the ultimate essential nature is investigated,
it consists solely of the triad beginning with the object of enjoyment (bhogya), and not the nature of his pastime-forms, mandalas, and so forth.
Since the maṇḍala and so forth, being of the nature of objects of knowledge (*vedya*), cannot logically possess the status of sense organs (*indriya*) or that of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*);

and since the objects of enjoyment and so forth, which are perceived in their specific forms, [are subsumed by] the *bindu*—which consists of the perception of the featureless (*nirviśeṣa*)—the *bindu* alone is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Thus, it is of the *bindu* itself...
This sixfold path is a modification. || 15 ||
To clarify this very point, he says:
"For this manifest world, consisting of objective entities, is eternally attached to that [Unmanifest];
and the unmanifest, consisting of potential power, again immerses itself into that very same [source]. (16)

This universe is twofold: gross and subtle. The gross is called the manifest (vyakta), and the subtle is called power (śakti). Among these, that which is the manifest universe consisting of objective entities is indeed eternal.
The ascendant at the time of birth is always the ascendant of the power of the bindu (*bindu-śakti*) during the various periods starting from the rising;
furthermore, that which is unmanifest and consists of power (*śaktyātmaka*) also merges therein.
Whatever exists as the universe, whether perceived in its gross or subtle form, [is contained within it].

All of that is not possible by existing outside of consciousness, whose nature is reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), just as waves and the like cannot exist outside of water; such is the meaning. || 16 ||

Now, some worship this very *citi* by conceptualizing it as "various" (*vividhā*) in view of the various kinds of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), [claiming] that there is no other distinct entity to be worshipped; therefore, he says:

Those wise ones who seek to attain success divide this [reality] sixteenfold, ninefold, sixfold, and also threefold, according to the distinctions of its substrata, which is characterized by manifold accomplishments. (17)

This drop (bindu), whose form has been thus established, is characterized by its various substrates; it is conceived as the object of perception within the diverse substrates beginning with the sixteenfold [cakras]. For this very reason, it bestows many supernatural powers (siddhis).

Practitioners seeking to achieve various forms of accomplishment through the limiting condition of the diversity of supports divide the support into sixteen ways and contemplate it as having a sixteen-fold nature within those sixteen supports; likewise:

[They are] ninefold, sixfold, and threefold. The application of the sixteenfold and other divisions to the supports (*ādhāra*) is due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), because no division is possible within their own essential nature (*svarūpa*). The intention of one who says "they will be established" is as follows:

Only those who are limited yogins (*mitayogin*), whose accomplishment of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of this true nature has not been attained, worship in this way through differentiation; but the perfected ones (*siddha*) do not. For they consist solely of the flavor of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), characterized by the firm realization of the identity of consciousness (*cidaikya*). They [are] consciousness—
