[Now the third chapter:

By this much of the composition, the nature of the Self as the essence of the universe has been established through its being supported by both reasoning and experience. Now, for one who has attained certainty—

The third book is commenced so that there may be no defilement arising from the impossibility of [the Lord's] being the self of all, or from contrary conceptions; therein, by the statement "residing in me," which characterizes the relationship between the support and the supported, this distinction [is addressed].
This being well-known, he refutes it by means of an exchange:
"I alone am of the nature of light that never sets, amidst both lights and darkness;
abiding within, the lights and darknesses are within me, who am one. (22)

I am of the nature of light that never sets, consisting of eternally risen radiance; I am the one without a second, abiding within all those things considered to be lights— the instruments such as the intellect and so forth, as well as the sun and other luminaries— by virtue of being their very light.

I am their inner self by virtue of being manifest as light; likewise, because they are manifest as darkness, I abide within the darknesses such as *bindu*, *māyā*, and so forth. For I, whose nature is light, am situated within them.
The intention of the Sun is that light should shine as light and darkness as darkness;
yet those lights and those darknesses reside within me,
and I alone am their illuminating self.
I manifest as the very form of the world, consisting of both existence and non-existence; therefore, there is no room whatsoever for the suspicion of duality—this is the intended meaning. || 22 ||

Having thus established the non-difference of consciousness alone with respect to the generality of the subject and with respect to the object, he says [the following] in order to discern the absence of difference in the appearance of the three aggregates— “that,” “you,” and “I”:
The three types of persons—the lowest, the middling, and the highest—are distinct from one another; yet, they do not exist apart from me, the Great Person, whose nature is self-reflective awareness.

These three persons— the first, the middle, and the highest— who are mutually distinct due to their association with heterogeneous designations such as "he," "you," and "I," and whose forms are mutually excluded from one another— all these indeed [are as follows].

Because the nature of reflective awareness (pratyavamarśa) persists [within me], no great being exists outside of me; there is no other reality distinct from me. Although these beings, beginning with the first person, possess mutually exclusive forms, [they do not exist apart from this awareness].

Because its nature consists of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), and because its creation and liberation are dependent on Me, as well as because it is perceived as having My single essence upon My "wall" (the ground of consciousness), it does not exist outside of Me. // 23 //

But surely, you are delimited as "I" by being the counter-correlative of the first and middle persons, and yet you are of the nature of undivided light. If there is such a difference, how can there be oneness? To this, he says:
That distinct form which appears here as "I," characterized by the exclusion of "you" and the exclusion of the "remainder," is merely a differentiation of parts; for I am one and eternal.
(24) [This applies] both to that which consists of the exclusion of "you" and to that which consists of the exclusion of the "remainder."
The meaning is that it is excluded from both the middle and the first persons.

For this very reason, that which appears as the form "I" shines forth as distinct, being the counter-correlative of those two. This is like [the expressions] "that" (*saḥ*) when there is a distinction of parts, or like "you" (*tvam*).

I am a certain particular portion of my own self, but I am not [the whole], nor is that my ultimate nature. The reason for this is: I am one, eternally so; I am eternally a single, undivided mass of uninterrupted light.
For this reason: My true nature is essentially light, eternal, and real because it is undivided; whereas the form "I" is adventitious because it is divided.
The meaning is that, as stated in such passages, [the object] is indeed a specific part [of the whole]. || 24 ||
And just as the subject, even when analyzed in detail,
is but a portion of myself, so too the object, when analyzed in detail, is but the expansion of my own power; thus he says:
The two powers of manifestation and concealment belonging to my multitude of states of being are those whose expansion constitutes space and time, and day and night, [respectively]. (25)

That which is space— namely heaven and earth— and that which is time— namely day and night— this pair of objects of cognition, which encompasses all other internal objects of cognition, has its manifestation solely through me, who am the cause of the appearance and disappearance of the multitude of existents.

Regarding the powers: that which is the manifestation and that which is the concealment of the entire multitude of objects are indeed my own powers. It was stated previously that the manifestation of objects is truly the unfolding of my power, while their differentiation is their concealment.

"By means of the conjunction and separation of the waves of its own powers, it creates and destroys" (verse 13). And thus, this space and time are the expansion of those very two powers of entities which consist in their manifestation and concealment.
He exists as both the counter-positive of existence and the counter-positive of non-existence;
the meaning is that he does not exist as something external to me. || 25 ||
Having indicated another function [of the powers] through manifestation (*bhāna*) and concealment (*tirodhāna*), he demonstrates it by specifically distinguishing them:
"In concealment, Dhūmāvatī and Hlādā; in manifestation, Puṣṭi and Bhāsvatī."
In agitation there is the power of vibration (parispanda), and in pervasion there is the power called the all-pervasive (vibhvī); thus, there are five powers. || 26 ||

Dhūmāvatī is my power in the first [state], Puṣṭi in nourishment, Hlādā in refreshment, Bhāsvatī in illumination, Spandā in agitation and vibration, and Vibhvī in pervasion— these are my five powers. || 26 ||
Since the powers (*śakti*) are not perceptible, their essential nature is determined solely through their effects; with this in mind, he defines them by way of their effects:
"The power *dhūmāvatī* manifests in earth, *hlādā* in water, and *bhāsvatī* in fire."
In the wind there are vibrations, and in the ether the world is pervaded by them. || 27 ||

And this being so, the entire universe, consisting of the six paths (*ṣaḍadhvan*), is pervaded by these five powers of mine, beginning with Dhūmāvatī, and is embraced by them. By this, [it is shown that] at all times—

It should be understood that the fivefold activity of the conscious self (cidātman) has been demonstrated. For instance: manifestation is emission (sṛṣṭi); stabilization is agitation (kṣobha); withdrawal is concealment (tirodhāna), which is expressed by its own name; and pervasion is grace (anugraha). || 27 ||

He says that the world, thus produced by manifestation and the other [powers], attains the state of being a single ocean of light through the mere touch of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), [referring to] "his own substrate" (*nijadharmiṇam*).

With these four verses beginning with "ityādibhiḥ" and ending with "kārtsnyenāviṣṭamiva," [the author] characterizes his own nature as Light; [he states: "The power whose form is reflective awareness (vimarśa), belonging to me, constitutes the body of this entire class of manifested objects. (28)
My power, whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is this consciousness (*citi*) whose form is self-reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*).

It makes the entire universe—from Śiva down to the earth—its own body, bringing it to a state of identity with me alone. Of what sort is it? [It is that which] possesses its own inherent attributes...

[She] makes manifest the consciousness— which is her own self, which has become the Dharma, and which is the light that serves as the foundational substratum for its own arising, dissolution, and so forth, and whose sole nature is apprehension— thereby establishing it as the essential nature of the entire range of objects to be manifested, and [thus] as the ultimate reality of the multitude of knowable things.
Establishing that the ultimate, unassailable, and remaining nature of this entire range of objects of knowledge is indeed Light itself, she demonstrates—
attested by her own experience— that she is the "I," whose very form is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
The power of consciousness renders this entire path, beginning with Śiva, as belonging to me alone. || 28 ||
For instance:

"The entire world, consisting of the knower, the act of knowing, and the object known, having been consumed by the flame of my own self-reflection, leaves behind only a pure ash in the form of light. (29)

This reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which is the crest of the flame of my own fire of reflective awareness, is perceived as a flame that pervades all paths (*adhvan*) by means of its form that pervades the self of all things.
Such is this reflective awareness of mine.
Having burned away the entire triad consisting of the knower, the act of knowing, and the object known,
and having instantly obliterated the specific attributes such as "knowership" and so forth, [it remains] pure, consisting of light and the universal nature of luminosity.

Because it is a mass of uncreated bliss, it leaves behind only the ash—the manifestation of pure existence—untainted by afflictions and the like; it renders everything into a single ocean of that alone. || 29 ||

Is it not the case that immediately following reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), the dissolution of duality occurs within the objective aspect (*vedyāṃśa*)? However, in the subjective aspect (*grāhakāṃśa*),
because the agent of the act of reflection remains distinct, this [dissolution] never occurs.
To explain the cessation of the subtle fraction of differentiation (*bhedakalā*), he says:
"The manifestation [of the world] remains concealed, swallowed by the crest of the flame of non-dual awareness (*advimarśa*), which is not yet harsh;
therein the group of atoms (*aṇuvarga*) spreads forth like ashes, as it were, [upon glowing] coals. (30)
In that context, when the entire sphere of the knower, the knowledge, and so forth has been set forth,
and everything has been consumed by the flame-tips of non-dual awareness (*advimarśa*), I have reflected upon the "I" (*aham*); for in this aspect of "I," no trace of duality remains.

When the group of limited subjects (*aṇuvarga*) is overcome by my own reflective awareness (*mad-vimarśa*), whose power of burning is not fully manifest, their appearance consists of the residual cognition "I" belonging to the group of perceivers.
Of what nature is this? It is characterized by concealment (*tirodhimat*), insofar as its state of being an object of knowledge has been withdrawn.

Enveloped by differentiation, which spreads inseparably from the aspect of the object of knowledge, it manifests like glowing coals or like ashes; it is perceived as being like a mass of subtle embers situated within. || 30 ||
If that burning is indeed intense, then he says: "Behold!

Just as a forest, a city, or the like is pervaded in its entirety by fire, so too does the world, when I [the yogi] am present, cast off its manifold diversity and assume a single uniform nature. (31)

This entire universe, from Śiva down to the level of the earth, has been completely pervaded and scrutinized without remainder by me, whose nature is the reflective awareness that unifies all distinctions, as if by fire.

Having cast off all internal distinctions and specific differences— just as a painting of a forest, city, and so forth, when viewed as a whole— is submerged within itself and assumes a single form, becoming a solid mass of pure light alone.
By the word "nanu" (surely), he reveals that this [self] is established by the experience of everyone. || 31 ||

It has been stated that when the world is entered by investigation in its entirety, the delusion of all duality comes to rest. He now demonstrates that very manner of complete entry by analyzing it in detail: (—)
The inward-facing essential nature is the knowledge of the object to be known, while its knower is consciousness;
this consciousness, whose body is the knower, is one, and I am none other than it.
For here, entities possess two natures: one directed outward and one directed inward. Of these, the former is gross, differentiated, and non-ultimate; whereas that which is inward-directed is...
[The object] is subtle, of a continuous nature, and ultimate. This being the case,
that which is the internal, ultimate essential nature of an object of knowledge such as a jar is precisely the cognition "this is a jar," because the external form [is derived] from that.
Because it arises from that [consciousness], because it persists by being attached to that very wall [of consciousness], and because it dissolves back into that same place;

whereas for this [object], its knower— the subject who is the very cause of the arising and persistence even of the cognition of a jar— is the inward-turned form consisting of the nature of the conceiving subject (*abhimantṛ*).

For consciousness, which is the nature of the knower and which, according to the aforementioned method, has attained the state of being a knower while remaining non-different from the object of knowledge, it is consciousness alone— consisting of self-reflective awareness— that is the most internal reality. And for this [consciousness], "I" is not other than consciousness itself.
When the aspect of reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) within that which is characterized by reflective awareness is submerged,
that which remains as the essence of pure light— namely "I"— is said to be the one [reality]. Thus,
it has already been established that "I" alone is the reality that has reached the ultimate limit (*kāṣṭhāprāpta*), and nothing else.
There is no object whatsoever distinct from me.
Prior to the arising of the conceptual construction "this is a jar" immediately following the contact of the sense organ with its object, there is neither the jar nor its status as a jar.

Because it is impossible to designate the object of knowledge as a separate entity, its inward-facing essential nature is knowledge itself. Since the arising and dissolution of knowledge also depend solely upon the knower, the knower alone is the most intimate form [of all].

By this very method, even the knower is nothing but consciousness; and of consciousness as well, I alone am the non-figurative reality. Thus, when one is immersed in the fire of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in its entirety, the state of being a single nature is beyond dispute.
It is thus taught that [the cognition] occurs simultaneously with the manifestation of the apprehended object and so forth. || 32 ||

Having thus established the absence of difference among the triad of the object of knowledge and the rest with respect to their manifestation, he analyzes how there is likewise no difference whatsoever between them mutually: (— )
Successive cognition and the rest do not belong to me; rather, consciousness is both successive and non-successive.
Like me, the knower is [consciousness]; knowledge is like power; and the object of knowledge is like the triad [of these]. || 33 ||

For me, whose ultimate nature is non-sequential light, there is indeed a state of non-sequentially (akramatvam) with respect to the fourfold [principles] beginning with consciousness, as well as with respect to myself; for,
since it is the form that permeates everything, even a trace of differentiation is impossible.

The triad beginning with the knower—namely, the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—is sequential, because it is perceived as having mutually distinct forms. Consciousness (cit), however, is both sequential and non-sequential: it is sequential in relation to the knower and so forth, and non-sequential in relation to itself.
"Succession is thus twofold. These are the modes of cognition for you who are awakened.
But in reality, just as I am a knower because of my persistence through the fourfold group beginning with consciousness (*cit*), so too [is the case for You].
Due to the persistence of knowledge and the object of knowledge, with respect to both of them as well as with respect to me,
the knower is without succession. Just as consciousness, like power (*śakti*),
appears to have succession in relation to the intellect, the knower, and so forth, yet is without succession in relation to me.

Likewise, knowledge also possesses succession in relation to the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), yet it is without succession in relation to me; thus it is like power (*śakti*). There is also the triad consisting of the object of knowledge, the knower "I," and knowledge itself—namely, the power and the other object of knowledge.

This triad should be understood as possessing a threefold nature. Just as the knower (*jñātṛ*) and the object known (*cetya*) are non-sequential (*akrama*), so too, in relation to us, the object known is non-sequential. By this very method, with respect to power (*śakti*) and knowledge (*jñāna*), it is both sequential and non-sequential.

The delusion that consciousness (cit), by depending on both [the knower and the known], possesses a dual nature is thereby dispelled; for there is no distinct ontological category (tattvāntara) such as "I am the knower," "consciousness," "power," or "the threefold object of knowledge. Herein lies the intended meaning: in cases such as "this is a forest," and so forth...
In comparison with everything, there is only the persistence of the forest; and in comparison with the forest, there is only the persistence of the trees;

thus, there is non-difference everywhere. However, when there is the cognition "mango" or "campaka," then, in comparison with the forest, there is the persistence of the mango and the campaka, and thus there is no difference [between them].
However, from the perspective of mutual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), there is indeed a distinction.
Thus, even in the present case, there is no difference between the totality (*samaṣṭi*) and the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) with respect to the Light (*prakāśa*);
yet, from the perspective of their mutual relation, they abide in their respective positions as appropriate. Therefore:

The state of following a sequence everywhere, sequentiality, and duality are excluded; thus, identity with Light alone is the ultimate reality, while differentiation is merely the play of non-reflection. || 33 ||
He demonstrates this very point by analyzing it:
"For in the case of yellow and other [colors], there is no blue; and in those cases, visual cognition shines forth.
It is not present in auditory and other cognitions; yet the knower persists as a common factor among them. (34)

Regarding what was stated—that the object of cognition (*jñeya*) is necessarily sequential in relation to other objects of cognition—he says the following to provide an illustration: "For when there is the apprehension 'this is yellow' with respect to yellow and so forth, blue is not [present];
for at that time, blue does not exist. Thus, because they possess mutually exclusive forms..."

The object of knowledge is indeed successive when considered in relation to other objects of knowledge. As for what was stated—that the power of cognition is both successive and non-successive—he demonstrates this:
"And here, visual cognition shines forth with respect to those [objects], such as yellow and so on, and with respect to this blue. It does not [shine forth] otherwise.

Regarding auditory and other [sensory] cognitions: that auditory cognition is indeed produced by hearing, and that visual [cognition] is produced by sight. Thus, because it occurs both successively and simultaneously, it is logical that cognition is like power (*śakti*).
As for what was stated, "the knower is like me," he says this to explain its meaning: "the knower."

And it is present within them; that is, within those visual objects such as yellow, blue, and so forth, and here, within those beginning with the auditory [objects]. Therefore, because its form persists everywhere, it is also established that it is known like "I. || 34 ||
Since the determination of the nature of reality is thus, therefore [the object] consists of a triad: myself as the knower, knowledge, and power; furthermore, there is the knowable.
For one who meditates without conceptual construction, that "I," that "she," and those three are all one.

For one who meditates upon me as the non-conceptual Knower, I— by the method already stated— become that [very Knower] because the cause of conceptualization is impossible; through the cessation of the latent impressions of duality by virtue of the identity with the light of the Knower, there arises an internal, firm realization.
For one who practices [this], accomplishment arises, characterized by the disappearance of the delusion regarding their difference.
Likewise, for one who meditates on knowledge as power (*śakti*) in a non-conceptual manner,
that [accomplishment] occurs through the very method previously described, by means of strengthening the meditation on the non-difference of power and knowledge.
The accomplishment consists in the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of their non-difference. Thus,
for one who meditates upon that triad as being once again the object of knowledge,
those three are [realized] through the knower and the light of consciousness— the power and the knowledge— of the object to be known.

The accomplishment consisting in the uprooting, along with its very roots, of this insurmountable delusion of duality—which persists together with other objects of knowledge—occurs immediately. In this regard, the verb "exists" (*bhavati*) and so forth applies to all three of these sentences: "I am that," "She is that," and "That triad is that."
It is not, however, that identity is being asserted; rather, it is the very nature of identity itself that has been made known.
Therefore, this oneness of theirs is not something to be proven, but is recognized as eternally established by the arguments already stated.
Thus has it been explained by the Teacher. || 35 ||
In this regard, he teaches that because the knower’s succession is due to eternal limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), his identity with the Light is eternally established:
"When there is the flow of another mental continuum (*santāna*), the knower appears as distinct and is successive."
Through union with me, that which is called the individual soul (jīva) becomes like me, appearing as if devoid of succession.
When a stream of yellow conceptualizations and so forth flows immediately after a single stream of blue conceptualizations and so forth, there is an appearance of differentiation.

The cognizer is sequential; because it apprehends by way of existing in a state of mutual exclusion— thinking "I am the illuminator of blue" and "I am the illuminator of yellow"— it is the grasper (grāhaka).
It possesses succession. When there is such sequentiality, at that very time this [entity] called the "living soul" (jīva)—which in reality is Śiva—is designated as "jīva" only for that duration.
However, this sequentiality which exists in me through union with me is solely due to the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the object of knowledge.
In reality, however, because it illuminates both blue and yellow,
being ever-present and pervading all things, my nature as the supreme light consists in the realization: "I am indeed always of the nature of the light that pervades everything."

Through yoga, characterized by the investigation of reality, there arises a non-sequential manifestation due to contact, just as it is with me. Just as light always shines without sequence, so too does the subject. In that very [state]...

At the time of perceiving yellow and other colors, [the object] appears simultaneously as one with the light of consciousness. By this, whenever the awakened one possesses the state of being the correlate of the universe, at that very moment he is Śiva; but when...

The delusion that persists— the notion that the impression (*saṃskāra*) of being a living being always continues because the state of being a grasper consists in the opposition to a specific object, and thus does not transcend these two forms— is utterly dispelled by the reasoning already stated.

It is taught that even during the state of perceiving yellow and other colors, [the cognition] possesses the nature of Śaṅkara, consisting of a non-sequential, complete, and single dense manifestation. || 36 ||

Now, as long as there is the conceptualization of two levels— namely, "the object of knowledge" (*vedyam*) as being distinct from consciousness and "consciousness" (*vedanam*) itself— as long as that duration of time remains devoid of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*),
so long do the object and the act of knowing persist. But when reflective awareness is brought forth, [they no longer exist].
He teaches that neither [subject nor object] exists as something external to the Light:

"The object of knowledge, having entered into the consciousness that pierces its own succession—the limbs, objects, and so forth—becomes characterized by that [consciousness] when it is dissolved into the knower through the gateway of consciousness. (37)

The object of knowledge consists of the limbs of the body, the sense-objects such as sound and so forth, the locus of experience, and the objects of enjoyment, including the body and its sensations. There is a distinction [in perception] solely by virtue of the object itself, according to the principle that "there is no difference among cognitions because they are formless," as one enters into a consciousness pierced by its own sequential order. This is the nature of the object.
The cognition, assuming the form of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), enters into the act of awareness;

then, upon the cessation of the sensory operation due to the subsiding of the curiosity of grasping, it attains the nature of awareness itself through the realization: "The cognition of yellow has arisen in me. Now, [regarding] the knower...
Having made the dissolution of the intellect itself its primary focus, [the mind] dissolves at the time of the intellect's dissolution into that which is well-known [as the Unmanifest].
Being thus dissolved, it acquires the characteristics of that [Unmanifest],
just as a bubble and the like, having dissolved into the ocean by way of the dissolution of the wave, attain identity with it.

In reality, it relies solely on that which exists. Here, because it is precisely the Light (prakāśa) itself that flashes forth as the universe—the nature of which consists of the reality of Śiva and so forth, its arising, its persistence, and its various manifestations—nothing whatsoever is perceived that exists outside of the Light. No.

It neither arises nor is it employed. Therefore, the very emergence of the conceptual constructions of the knower, feeling, and so forth— which, like waves and the like, are non-different from that [reality]—
is itself the existence of the entity consisting of the knower and so on.

The arising and so forth of that [consciousness], as well as its differentiation, constitute this very reality. The essential point of the teaching is that Śiva-hood consists precisely in such reflective awareness (vimarśa); intense reflective awareness is awakening, whereas the absence of reflective awareness is the state of a bound soul (paśutva). || 37 ||

Now, just as the first [objection] regarding the knower was raised and refuted by the verse beginning with "that you" (*sa tvam*)— on the grounds that he is the object of cognitions such as recognition (*pratyaya*), starting with "the first, the middle" (verse 23)— in exactly the same way, [an objection may be raised] regarding the known object on the grounds that it is the object of cognitions such as memory.
Anticipating the objection regarding difference, he refutes it:
"By virtue of the connection between memory and direct experience, this world appears as such;
and by means of exclusion (apohana), I, the self-abiding illuminator, manifest it as distinct from one another. (38)
By virtue of memory it is "that," and by virtue of direct experience it is "this";
the synthesis [of these] is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). By virtue of that, [the yogi realizes]: "I am Śiva and so forth; I am the world;
I am the self-sustaining illuminator; I am the independent creator. How so?

"Different" means distinct from one another through mutual exclusion (*apohana*), and by the word "and," it also implies non-different. This is the power of His sovereignty. Because mutual exclusion consists in the form of constant mutual differentiation, [He says: "I create as different."
When reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśana*) has been performed by means of the aforementioned arguments,

[the object] is [perceived] as non-different because of the disappearance of its exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); for reflective awareness has the singular nature of swallowing various moments of exclusion (*nimeṣa*) that consist of differentiation.

For when reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is slackened, there arises the emergence of differentiated forms such as "this" or "that"; however, when reflective awareness is fully established, because distinctions such as "that" and so forth dissolve, there is the sovereign empire of pure light alone—this is the intended meaning. || 38 ||

For one who, according to the stated method, relies upon manifestation alone as the foundational support and does not admit the arising, dissolution, and so forth of these various distinctions precisely because they are non-different from it;
The proponent of difference states the subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*):
"Recollection, the manifestation of experience, and that [manifestation] of the object—
these three, when synthesized together, cannot possibly exist as a single unity devoid of me and lacking in sequence, even for the wise."
The manifestation of experience— that is, this manifestation of a cognition whose object is a thing such as "this is blue"— is a memory in relation to that object such as blue.
That experience, which serves as the basis for the memory "that [object] is this," is what is being referred to.

In the phrase "of the object" (*arthasya*), the word "manifestation" (*bhānam*) is carried over [from the previous context]. Thus, the meaning is that the manifestation of the object is experience (*anubhava*). Both of these—recollection and experience—are together [the two types of cognition].

At the moment of reconnecting with an object previously perceived, the state of becoming a single cognition is called "recollection" (*anusandhāna*) or "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*). This triad, though appearing sequential, is devoid of sequence and is not possible without me, the one [Self].
Therefore, the single light that is woven through all objects of cognition would not be possible without it; for if a non-sequential light that synthesizes everything were not admitted, then...
The meaning is that even such [arguments] as "this is intended to be gradual" would result in a painting without a foundation (nirbhittika). || 39 ||
Since this is so, therefore:
The multitude of objects, having shone forth as if distinct and then ceased their manifestation, remains within me like a river in the ocean, through its identity with my own consciousness. (40)

The collection of objects, appearing as if divided though in reality division is impossible, obstructs even the cognition of "this blue" at the moment of its subsiding; it conceals the blue within the light [of consciousness]. Being thus situated...
But it exists in identity with my own nature; the sense is that even the entire collection of objects ultimately becomes nothing other than the nature of light itself. || 40 ||
[Thus ends the third chapter, the Section on Contemplation (*vimarśaskandha*), in the *Śrīvirūpākṣapañcāśikā*, together with its commentary.]

[Now the Fourth Section] Now, the fourth section, the Section on Manifestation (*vibhūti-skandha*), is to be commenced. In that regard, as a limb for the manifestation of manifestation, for those who are unawakened and so forth—

The manner of realization is first examined by means of four verses beginning with "Even that which resides within me... and so forth. In this regard, there are five types: the unawakened, the one resembling the awakened, the awakened, the one resembling the well-awakened, and the well-awakened.
The knowers [of reality]. He shows, by distinguishing them, what kind of cognition each of them possesses:
"By means of Māyā, the multitude of worlds, though residing within me, appears as if external to me."
For those who possess existence, then through knowledge there would be the state of being both internal and external for those who have entered into existence. 41.
Even though the multitude of worlds— from Anāśrita down to Kālāgni— rests upon me as my very wall by virtue of its nature as manifestation according to the logic already stated,
that circle of worlds appears to transmigrating beings as if it were external to me. This is *bhava*.

The apprehension of difference [occurs] regarding those who hold the tenets of the Sāṃkhya and others. The reason for this is "by means of illusion" (māyayā)—that is, by means of an illusion whose nature is the perception of difference within a reality that is actually non-different. However, for those who have reached the state of existence (bhavapadinām), there is no such existence.

But for those who abide in the state of becoming (*bhava*), there exists that form consisting of residual impressions (*saṃskāra*) which is the locus of becoming; these are the knowers of reality (*vidyā-pramātāraḥ*) who have entered the stages prior to *samprajñāta-samādhi*.
By virtue of being internal and external, it appears as if divided through the form of internal volition and so forth; the reason for this is "by means of pure *vidyā*. (41)
Now, he says that between these two, whoever appears as external is the "bound soul" (paśu), fit for this instruction on consciousness:
"He who considers the subject alone to be non-inert and everything else to be inert and the object of his perception..."
That atomic being, whose self is deluded by māyā, should be awakened by the virtuous. 42.
The grasper is non-inert and consists of consciousness; the grasped is inert and consists of non-consciousness. He who perceives anything else [besides this] has a self deluded by māyā;
this is that perception of the object intended as the grasped as being both inert and other.
That very [power] is Māyā; by it, his self is deluded and his true nature is not recognized.

For this very reason, he is a *bhavin* (one subject to worldly existence), who must be awakened by the wise, and an *anu* (individual soul), who is a *paśu* (bound beast) to be instructed by Gurus whose own true nature has been recognized.
As for the scriptural authority (āgama):
"Those persons who, in other tantras, are liberated through the exhaustion of dharma and adharma, are here called Rudrāṇavas, being devoid of [the influence of] time and karma. Thus it is said.
By this,

it is taught that logicians, Mīmāṃsakas, and others— who have not recognized the true nature of consciousness as distinct from the objects of thought— have no qualification whatsoever for the instruction of the authentic scriptures.
It is so. Regarding the revelation of the doctrines established by direct experience (*saṃvitsiddhānta*) among those [uninitiated], there is a scriptural injunction concerning the transgression:
"One who speaks contrary to the rule shall meet death at an untimely hour.
Therefore, the meaning of the doctrines established by direct experience must be concealed from the uninitiated (*paśu*); this is the command of Śiva.
In every respect, it must certainly not be transgressed. || 42 ||

Thus, the manner of cognition for one who is unawakened and for one who is like the awakened has been analyzed and shown. Now, however, he analyzes that which belongs to the awakened one: namely, this "thisness" (*idantā*) whose nature is insentience (*jaḍatā*), and the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) whose nature is non-insentience (*ajaḍatva*).
Through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the two-footed [consciousness] perceives "this am I.
Due to the influence of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of both worldly existence and its emergence,
that which abides in the state of difference-and-non-difference perceives the insentient nature of "this-ness" as "this."
The inert object being perceived, as well as the non-inert "I-ness" (ahantā) and the non-inert "I-object" (aham-vastu) being perceived,
are cognized as "this is I" by superimposing non-difference through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), thereby submerging the aspect of difference.
One perceives [the world] in two forms, by way of its identity with one's own body; this is the state of the Lord (īśvaradaśā).

Now, he analyzes the manner of comprehension regarding both the "one who is well-awakened" (*suprabuddha*) and the "state of being well-awakened" (*suprabuddhatva*): for those who have arisen [from that state], the submerged [reality] shines within the state [of consciousness] by means of a vision that is purely [intuitive].

Furthermore, within me, who am full, there is the emergence of liberation characterized by the realization of non-duality— a state that is both submerged and emerged, and beyond the mind (*unmanā*). For those who possess this realization,
it shines forth as submerged within the internal state of the self-nature, which consists of the "I" (*ahamātman*).
This object of perception, the knowable that has been blinked, is perceived by what cause?

By the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) through the vision. This is the state of Sadāśiva, consisting of an indistinct sense of "this-ness" (*idantā*) veiled by "I-ness" (*ahantā*). Therefore, in me, the light, who am perfectly awakened and for that very reason full.

It is perceived as having two forms— both submerged and emerged— by virtue of being closed and open respectively. For just as waves and the like in the ocean are both closing and opening, yet in every state they remain nothing but the ocean itself.

Thus, the entire universe, beginning with Śiva, unfolds as being essentially identical to me, and it dissolves back into me alone, being nothing other than me. This is the means for the recognition of the true nature of reality: by means of the *unmanā* state.
Abiding in one's own true nature is indeed *unmanā*, as the scripture states:
"That is to be known as *unmanā* wherein the mind (*manas*) is not found. (44)

When the yogi, reflecting upon the sequence of realization thus taught, attains through *unmanā* the unwavering perfection of fullness (*pūrṇatva*), then that yogi is called a perfected one (*siddha*) and is said to be "well-awakened" (*suprabuddha*). By his mere will, [he attains] those things he desires...
He explains that the manifestation of supernatural powers (*vibhūtis*) occurs through eight verses.

Therein, he elaborates upon the manner in which other accomplishments (*siddhis*) manifest: "By means of the sun, moon, lightning, thunderbolt, clouds, submarine fire, ocean, mountain caves, and forests..."
The yogi, whose self-nature has been firmly cultivated, accomplishes that action. || 45 ||
The *vajra* is the thunderbolt. By means of those [planets] such as the Sun, whose natures have been firmly cultivated—that is, firmly conceived as being the self—the yogi accomplishes that activity;
whatever activity there may be, such as the illumination of the world, among the objects such as the Sun and others.

The meaning is that that very reality, which is eternally established as such, attains a fulfillment characterized by causal efficacy (*arthakriyākāritā*) through the firmness of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
Herein lies the underlying intention (*ākūta*): according to the aforementioned method, [it exists] in the form of objects such as the sun and so forth.
It abides in itself alone; however, due to the weakness of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), it remains as if divided.

When the latent impressions of the delusion of duality are removed by powerful reflective awareness, all accomplishments (*siddhi*) are eternally established for that which exists as the self of the universe.
Since [cognitions] become capable of purposeful action through the firmness of recognition,
one who desires to establish this everywhere must remain unwavering from one's own true nature, which consists of the supreme light that is all-pervasive and complete.

The venerable Gurus maintain that the meditation on [the self] as consisting of the sun and so forth must be brought to the point of being subordinate to the meditation on [the self] as consisting of all things. 45.
Whatever deity performs a particular purpose, for one who is intent upon that purpose and firmly maintains the ego-identification with that deity, that purpose is accomplished in an instant. || 46 ||

Whatever deity exists in the world— be it Heramba, Bhāratī, Hari, Hara, or others— whatever purpose they perform, such as the destruction of obstacles, the promotion of speech, protection, or withdrawal, [may that be accomplished].
It accomplishes the task; therefore, for the seeker— that is,
for one who possesses a purpose and desires to achieve that object—
he firmly maintains his ego within it, contemplating its identity with it through unwavering stability.
For the yogi, that object comes to him in an instant; that object is accomplished without delay. || 46 ||
Now, he describes the accomplishments (*siddhi*) therein:

"Through the elements characterized by retention, cohesion, maturation, expansion, and non-obstruction, when their respective 'I-ness' (*ahaṃtā*) is established, the desired activity of the yogin comes to pass. (47)
Earth has the characteristic of supporting; water has the characteristic of cohesion; fire has the characteristic of ripening;
and wind has the characteristic of diffusion, which is the joining together of parts.

Non-resistance, which is the state of having unimpeded movement— that is the characteristic of space. Through these five elements, each firmly perceived as one's own self, the desired action of the yogin comes to pass.
The accomplishment of the desired actions, such as the meditative concentration (dhāraṇā) and so forth, comes to pass. || 47 ||
Thus, [the ego] exists in the subtle elements (tanmātra), the organs of action, the organs of knowledge, the mind, and in the sense of "I" (asmitā);
likewise, it exists in the unmanifest (avyakta) and in the Person (puruṣa), where the power of consciousness (cit-śakti) is held, and its activity is directed toward that.

Asmitā is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*). Among these principles, beginning with the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and ending with the [unmanifest], the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), having been sustained by the ego-sense according to the very method already stated, is called *dhṛti*.
And he who possesses that [power] becomes one who accomplishes various specific actions. || 48 ||

In the same manner, those who have established their ego-sense (ahantā) reside in Rāga and Niyati; in Kāla, Vidya, and Kalā; in Guhā and Sarasvatī; in Īśa, Sadāśiva, and Śakti; and likewise in Śiva. || 49 ||
The cave is *māyā*; Sarasvatī is *śuddhavidyā*. The phrase "in that manner" draws back [the reference to] "her activity. || 49 ||
In this context, he states that the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) of Śuka and others are indeed minor:
"The divine nature (*vaiśvātmya*) born from the yoga of the elements and the self, as found in Śuka, Vāmadeva, Kṛṣṇa, Dadhīci, and likewise in Vainya, is indeed declared to be of the Ṛṣis. (50)

Born from the yoga of the self as the elements, arising from the concentration on the five elements, it is the universal nature (*vaiśvātmya*), having the form of the manifold expansion of the five elemental selves. This is stated in the *ārṣa* scriptures, such as the *itihāsas*. Among these aforementioned accomplishments (*siddhis*), those ending with the accomplishment of the cave (*guhāsiddhi*)—
The other five, which are different, are the supreme accomplishments beginning with Sārasvatī. || 50 ||
Now, with two verses, he speaks of the two accomplishments that are the pinnacle of all accomplishments:
"Blazing like ten million fires of cosmic destruction, she is skillful in burning away the accumulation of bonds and satisfied in her fullness."
Meditate upon Śakti, whose form is a downpour of a flood of nectar; become the Guru of the world.

[She is] like ten million fires of cosmic dissolution ignited at the time of universal destruction, capable of burning away all paths by virtue of her nature as an unbroken mass of flames blazing like ten million fires of cosmic dissolution.
Remember the sharp power capable of burning away the mass of bonds;

contemplate the unimpeded consciousness within the purification that consists of the burning away of the bond characterized by the six paths. Contemplate it as having the form of a downpour of floods of nectar during the state of satisfaction.
But regarding purification characterized by immersion,
remember clearly that it is likewise composed of the essence of a thousand oceans of unbroken nectar, capable of traversing all the paths of time; here, through both burning and immersion—
The process of sakalīkaraṇa is also indicated, as stated by the most eminent teachers:
"O Mother, who shines like ten million fires of cosmic destruction, during the purifications of the six paths, you pour down this rain of floods of nectar."
"By meditating upon her as dark-complexioned, with heavy breasts, and as the personification of all [mantras], one becomes a teacher of the worlds.
Thus, because it consists of millions of mental resolves (saṅkalpa) whose essence is the form of the chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā),...

It should also be understood that the sakalīkaraṇa (the ritual of making [the deity] complete), characterized by the contemplation of the universe, has been taught. Be a guru for the world; as much purification as has been performed for the entire path, so much [purification] is for the sake of bestowing grace upon the whole world without exception.

May the Guru be the most excellent of teachers. Herein lies the underlying intention: this purification which is performed is not for this contracted aggregate of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvan) consisting of the body alone, but rather for the entirety of all things.
According to the principle stated, since the teacher and all others possess the universe as their body,
this status of being a teacher and so forth does not consist in being an embodied soul limited to a specific body. Therefore,
while possessing the universe as one's body, the purification of the universe itself must be performed.

For one who perceives this entire universe as identical with the Light (*prakāśa*) through the sequence of arguments established by the scriptures, that abiding in one's own true nature (*svarūpa*) is the burning away of the entire path (*adhvan*).
And that very identity with the Light, when being contemplated, [is the state of liberation].

The immersion consisting of the wonder of consciousness (*ciccamatkāra*) is the manifestation of supreme bliss (*parānanda*), which arises from the firmness of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of the light [of consciousness] as a single mass of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); this is "the process of making everything one's own" (*sakalīkaraṇa*).
The venerable feet of the illustrious Yogīśvarācārya. || 51 ||
Having thus taught the supreme first accomplishment (*siddhi*), which consists of the acquisition of a guru, he now teaches the second as well:
"Through the firmness of absorption into the perfect manifestation (*pūrṇakhyāti*), [one attains] the incomplete manifestation (*khyāti*)."
Destroy!
Create the worlds as you desire; establish them, withdraw them, and illuminate them.
This is your essence, the quintessence of all instruction: incomplete, yet complete.
Thus, there are only these two manifestations, and no other reality. In this regard, by firmly grasping the manifestation of fullness as a real entity,
one should exhaust the incomplete manifestation— which is not a real entity— because it is merely occasional.
Uproot [them] through the firmness of your continuous contemplation at every moment.

Thus, while destroying them, create worlds as you desire, establish them, withdraw them, and illuminate them. For those [impurities] which, while you remain thus, act as veils to your own true nature—
The conceptual constructions (vikalpas) recognized as the powers of manifestation and so forth regarding objects are themselves,
when recognized as being of the nature of the creation of the universe and so on, will manifest supreme sovereignty, which consists of the totality of all accomplishments.

Therefore, "remain forever established in this very nature"—this is the quintessence of all instruction. Here, by stating that "the sun, the moon," and so forth, up to the manifestations ending with Śiva, "perform their respective functions," there is a revelation of [His] detachment; therefore, become the power of Smara (Kāma).
From the respectful instruction, "The Guru is the Lord of the world," and "Destroy the perception of incompleteness and create the worlds," his partiality is made known. For this very reason,
for one whose true nature has been thus recognized, other supernatural powers (*siddhi*) are merely appearances.

One should not harbor attachment to that; rather, it is taught implicitly that one must maintain an unwavering reflective awareness regarding the two-fold accomplishment that follows—may there be auspiciousness! 52.
Now, concluding the treatise,
he says: (53) Thus enlightened, that Indra, having cast off the impurity of his authority over the gods,
and with the principle of power (*śakti-tattva*) manifest within him, beheld his own self as Śiva.

Thus, having demonstrated with logical justification— by means of the first chapter— that the entities beginning with Śiva, which were previously considered external to the body, are in fact the body itself; then,
for the sake of purifying the state of being the body of the universe, by means of the second chapter, [the author establishes] them as the body.

Having established through logical arguments that the entire universe is a single mass of light, in order to dispel the delusion of duality characterized by the relationship of owned and owner regarding that which exists as the counter-correlative (pratiyogin), [the author proceeds] in that manner.
Lest the stability of the realized universal selfhood (*vaiśvātmya*) be weakened by defects such as contrary conceptions (*viparīta-bhāvanā*),
the third book [describes] various...

Having taught the methods for reflecting upon one's universal self-nature (*vaiśvātmya-vimarśana*), the fourth chapter [teaches] the recognition of the eternal perfection of the two great accomplishments (*mahāsiddhi*)— namely, being the teacher of the world and being Śiva— through the manifestation of spiritual power (*siddhi*).

Having been told of the great accomplishment that is without characteristics and is immovable, and having been correctly made to recognize the true nature of reality through awakening, that Indra cast off his impure authority over the gods, thinking, "I am the sovereign of heaven."
Having cast off the state of being a bound soul (paśutva), which is characterized by the contraction of one's own true nature,
he beheld his own self as Śiva; for Śiva, through His power of awakening, is the venerable teacher Virūpākṣanātha, standing before him— thus awakened was he.

Because no other Śiva is possible apart from the Guru, he perceived [the Guru] as such. There is not the slightest degree of difference in knowledge between these two—the object of knowledge and the knower—but rather [he realized]: "I am the Guru of this world, the Supreme Lord himself."
He attained freedom from all obstacles; may there be auspiciousness. || 53 ||

[Thus ends the fourth chapter, on Manifestations (*vibhūti*), in the *Śrīvirūpākṣapañcāśikā*, together with the commentary composed by the Great Lord of Maheśvara, the Sovereign of Knowledge (*vidyācakravartin*).]
Let this very clear commentary on the *Pañcāśikā* be studied by those who desire to effortlessly attain the recognition of one's own true nature (*svarūpa-pratyabhijñāna*).
This concise commentary has been composed by Śrī Vidyācakravartin;
it is set down upon the touchstone named the intellect of Govindacandra.
Homage to Śiva, the Guru, the God whose form is bliss;
to Śambhu, the God of gods, whose nature is the Supreme Brahman.
[And this treatise is completed.]
